passages.text: The question: What is the nature of time (kaal)? How does Madhyasth Darshan relate timeless Omnipresence (satta) to the duration of unit-activity, numerical reckoning, and the past–present–future structure — and how does that compare with Advaita Vedanta, philosophy of time, and modern physics (spacetime, cosmology, entropy)?

When water comes to the boil, a seed grows into a tree, or the Earth completes an orbit around the sun, two things are easy to conflate: the ongoing activity itself, which takes a definite span to unfold, and the clock or calendar numbers humans use to compare one span with another. If the clock reading is mistaken for a separate cosmic container through which things travel, time seems to exist on its own even apart from activity; if temporal change is treated as mere appearance, the reality of growth, responsibility, and human action is undercut.

This study develops the comparative treatment begun in The Ontology of Coexistence (§1.4, §2.7, §4.3). That paper states Madhyasth Darshan’s core claim — time (kaal) as the duration of activity, timeless Omnipresence (satta), and numerical reckoning within existence — and defers four connected questions to this study (Ontology §1.4): how past, present, and future arise from activity that is eternally present; how coexistence and the central faculty of the conscious self (atma) remain valid across all three times without cancelling the world; how this account compares with Advaita Vedanta’s three-time (trikaal) language; and how it stands beside McTaggart’s A- and B-series, presentism and eternalism, and modern physics (spacetime, cosmology, and entropy). Together these questions bear directly on human living: because present activity is where change actually occurs and where past configurations are carried forward, study (adhyayan), realisation (anubhav), and responsible conduct take place in an active present rather than a predetermined block or an illusory appearance.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1. The Madhyasth Darshan Answer

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan holds that time (kaal) belongs to the activity of units, not to Omnipresence as ground. To understand that claim, we must look past two common assumptions: the Newtonian view that time is an absolute cosmic container flowing independently of events, and the Advaitic view that time is an ultimate illusion (mithya). The darshan grounds time in the objective reality of nature (prakriti), defining it through the ongoing activity (kriya) of units (ikai).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.1 Time as the duration of activity

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan does not posit time as an independent dimension, substance, or background framework. Instead, whenever any bounded unit acts, moves, or transforms, that ongoing activity has a continuance or span, and that duration is what the darshan calls time (kaal):

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Time (kaal): Duration of an activity is referred to as time.” - MVD, p. 34

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Because every physical (jada) and sentient (chaitanya) unit in existence is eternally active through the single triad of effort, motion, and result (shram–gati–parinam) — in sentient jeevan read toward completeness through projection, reflection, and resolution (samadhan; The Ontology of Coexistence §1.2) — activity is perpetual. Time is the inseparable duration of this activity. It is not something units “move through”; it is a feature of their ongoing motion and state.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Time is measured by the duration of an activity.” - SB, p. 65

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Where there is no transforming activity, there is no time in this sense. That restriction applies directly to Omnipresence (satta).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2 Kaal, rachna, and vistar — a duration taxonomy

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In ordinary language, the span of an activity and the persistence or extent of a physical object are often run together. Madhyasth Darshan does not treat “duration” as one undifferentiated category; it distinguishes the duration of an activity from the boundedness and span of a material composition:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Time (kaal): Duration of an activity is referred to as time.” “Composition (rachna): The bounds of matter is referred to as composition or object, which is measured.” “Expanse (vistar): The span of a composition is referred to as expanse.” - MVD, p. 196

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Time (kaal) belongs to activity — the ongoing effort–motion–result (shram–gati–parinam) of units. Composition (rachna) and expanse (vistar) belong to bounded matter: how a composition holds together as a counted object and how far that composition extends. The duration of matter’s existential measure and form depends on its organisation and state (MVD, p. 41) — not on a freestanding temporal container.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Absolute energy (satta as uniform energy) is present in every time, place, and object; no place or object lacks it. Places devoid of matter are acknowledged, but no time devoid of that energy is proven (MVD, p. 41). Time (kaal) in the strict sense still applies only where activity occurs; matter-duration (rachna, vistar) tracks bounded configurations, not the ground.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3 The timelessness of Omnipresence (satta)

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Existence (astitva) is the inseparable coexistence of units and Omnipresence. While units have form and are ceaselessly active, Omnipresence (satta) is formless, all-pervasive, and entirely devoid of activity (kriya-shunya).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Because satta performs no actions and undergoes no change, duration in the sense of kaal does not apply to it. Omnipresence exists “at all places and times, and … [is] eternally present” (MVD, p. 34). That “all times” language names omnipresence, not temporal becoming in satta: there is no place or time where formless existence is absent (SB, p. 69). Omnipotence is present everywhere and at all times, and all unit-activities are encompassed within it — indivisible from it as regulation and supreme cause (mahakaran), not as an efficient trigger of particular change (MVD, p. 296; The Ontology of Coexistence §1.4).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: At the level of units (ikai), time is real as the duration of shram–gati–parinam. At the level of the ground (satta), there is absolute timelessness as actionless (kriya-shunya) completeness. The two levels are not contradictory because kaal is defined only through activity (kriya), not as a freestanding dimension in which satta sits.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: In awakened human living, kaal also carries a second, contextual sense naming the occasion of an activity: omnipresent satta becomes evident as law at the time of vocation, resolution at the time of thinking, bliss at the time of realisation, and justice at the time of behaviour (MVD, p. 34). These are modalities of human activity, not independent cosmic time — the same ground expressed in distinct phases of work, thought, experience, and conduct.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4 Trikaalabadh, atma, and timeless coexistence

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: If units are constantly active while the ground is actionless, what remains constant across past, present, and future? The harmony of consciousness and matter in coexistence holds across all three times:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “…a timeless truth valid across all three times.” - SB, p. 48

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The Sanskrit term trikaalabadh — uncontradicted or binding across past, present, and future — applies to coexistence as a whole (SB, p. 48), not to prove that unit-activity is illusory, but to show that what is understood about coexistence does not come and go with a passing moment. Existence does not begin and does not end; satta is atemporal as ground, yet coexistence holds across the three times. Time (kaal) as duration belongs to the activity of units, not to satta as an efficient cause (The Ontology of Coexistence §1.4).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: At the sentient level, the central faculty of the conscious unit (atma) likewise remains constant across all three times:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Atma exists in the form of mediative activity across all three times. Existence is unchanging; its realisation happens in atma, and enlightenment happens in buddhi.” - MVD, p. 299

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Atma is mediative activity — free from generative and degenerative pressure (MVD, p. 296). Its presence across the three times names the unchanging existential element in sentient nature, realised in atma and understood in buddhi, while unit-activity and kaal as duration continue in transforming nature. Uncontradicted validity across the three times (trikaalabadh) thus holds both for coexistence as the whole reality and for atma as the mediative core through which unchanging existence is realised, affirming three-time validity without sublating the world (SB, p. 48; MVD, p. 299).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This is Madhyasth Darshan’s answer to a question Advaita also faces with three-time (trikaal) language: how can the absolute be related to past, present, and future without being swallowed by temporal becoming? Madhyasth Darshan’s reply is a two-aspect ontology of coexistence — a timeless ground and temporally active units, with coexistence and atma holding true across the three times without cancelling the world.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.5 Relative truth, measurement, and numerical reckoning

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: To explain how time can be both an objective feature of activity and a human system of clocks and calendars, the darshan distinguishes three kinds of truth. Through awakening, one recognises absolute truth as nature saturated in Omnipotence, relative truth as direction, time, and place, and objective truth as form, properties, essential nature, and dharma (SB, p. 65). Time (kaal) enters as relative truth — alongside direction and place, not as absolute or objective truth in its own right:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Relative truth is evident in the form of direction, time, and place. … The duration of activity, as time, is a humanly devised numerical reckoning within existence.” - SB, p. 251

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Truth (satya) is defined as what is uniformly perceivable, existent, and realisable at all three times — the eternal presence (nitya vartaman) of absolute, relative, and objective truth in existence (MVD, p. 336). Time as relative truth is therefore real within coexistence — humans measure and coordinate activity-duration — while its numerical expression is a human convention:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “The measurement of time, expanse and different compositions is through mathematics.” - MVD, p. 195

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Every duration appears in numerical form when measured, and human purposes can be organised on the basis of time or activity (JVD, p. 85). In scientific and practical inquiry, time is associated with activity once comprehensive object-knowledge is established through analysis (JVD, pp. 160–161). Time-reckoning compares one activity against a standard reference activity (such as the Earth’s rotation or an atomic oscillation). The underlying duration of the activity is real; quantification and coordinate systems belong to human measurement within the knowledge order (gyan avastha), not to the fundamental ontology of satta.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.6 Activity eternally present and the three times

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan emphasises the present as the locus of causal reality, addressing the question deferred from The Ontology of Coexistence §1.4 of how past and future relate to present activity:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Every numerical moment of time, which is taken to be past or future, is found to be present in the form of activity. Thus, it becomes studiable that activity is eternally present.” - JVD, p. 85

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Read carefully, this is not a denial that humans experience past and future. We remember, anticipate, and plan; numerical reckoning distinguishes earlier and later durations. The claim is ontological and pedagogical: whatever moment we label past or future, studiable reality appears as present activity. In insentient nature, anticipated change appears as the projected result (parinam) of current effort–motion–result (shram–gati–parinam) activity; in sentient jeevan, the same triad continues toward resolution (samadhan) through projection and reflection rather than physicochemical parinam (The Ontology of Coexistence §1.2). Only present activity possesses causal efficacy in the darshan’s order of nature.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Where does the “past” survive if it is not an independent temporal place? In Madhyasth Darshan it persists in present forms at two levels. Physically, as inherited structural traces and configurations within material units (jada ikai) — consistent with conservation through transformation, not annihilation (The Ontology of Coexistence §1.4). In the human order, through the faculties of jeevan: chitta (sahaj chitran — natural visualisation) includes time (kaal) among its eight reckoning activities — form, property, count, time, expanse, effort, motion, and result (MVD, p. 327); buddhi’s innateness is enlightenment of time, activity, and truth (MVD, p. 204); sanskar carries acceptances and knowledge forward across cycles (MVD, p. 90; The Ontology of Coexistence §§1.6.1, 1.8). Through chitta and buddhi, past and future become numerically distinguishable categories for humans — not because duration ceases for insentient units, which have kaal as activity-duration without chitta, but because human study compares visualised durations against present activity (JVD, p. 85). The full map of mun, vritti, chitta, buddhi, and atma belongs in the ongoing study Philosophy-Of-Mind-And-Jeevan; this paper notes only what time requires from that structure.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Activity eternally present” therefore names two related truths: (1) units never cease their activity (kriya); (2) the human study of time, activity, and the present becomes coherent when we stop treating past and future as independent places and instead trace them to ongoing activity now. This is closer to present-centred process ontology than to eternalism, but it is not identical to Western presentism, because the past is real as completed activity (trace, configuration, and human reckoning through chitta, buddhi, and sanskar) rather than as sheer non-being.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.7 Place, time, and eternal presence

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Questions that treat place and time as containers into which existence must be fitted — for example, asking where the four orders “were” before Earth formed — rely on container constructs that do not apply to existence as a whole. In the intrinsic magnificence of existence, characterised by eternal presence (nitya vartaman), place and time do not interfere (SB, p. 103). Existence is not limited to place or time; its magnificence is beyond those constraints, even though humans express reality through words and imagine places and times speculatively (SB, p. 138).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: That claim complements, rather than contradicts, the reality of kaal as activity-duration and of relative truth as direction, time, and place. At the unit level, direction, place, and measured duration are operationally valid — mutual reference points among units (ikai) and numerical reckoning of activity (SB, p. 65). At the existential level, existence (astitva) is eternally present (nitya vartaman): what was, continues to be; what was not, does not happen (SB, p. 103). Place and time as human reckoning frameworks coordinate activity within coexistence; they do not bound or originate existence itself.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.8 The primacy of the present

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Because units are always in effort–motion–result (shram–gati–parinam) now, the present is the actualised state of existence. Madhyasth Darshan refuses both the Advaitic sublation of temporal becoming at the highest truth and the block-universe picture on which all moments are equally real and static. Change is ontologically real; the present is where transformation occurs. Numerical time is how humans coordinate that reality across scales — from atomic cycles to cosmic epochs — without reifying time as a container independent of activity.

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2. The Advaita Vedanta Answer

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta holds that existence in the absolute sense (paramartha) is Brahman alone — beginningless, changeless, partless, and entirely outside temporal becoming (VC, v. 393).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.1 Time at vyavahara and paramartha

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Upanishads place the absolute both within and beyond temporal structure. The Mandukya Upanishad opens by defining the ultimate reality (represented by Om) as encompassing all temporal phases and transcending them:

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “This letter that is Om is all this. Of this a clear exposition (is started with): All that is past, present, or future is verily Om. And whatever is beyond the three periods of time is also verily Om.” - MU, v. 1

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Time (kaal) is a structural feature of the empirical world (vyavahara). At this level, past, present, and future, causal succession, and birth and death are operationally valid. Time governs the physical universe and is wielded by Ishvara (Saguna Brahman) as cosmic force of transformation and dissolution:

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “I am the world-destroying Time, grown in stature…” - BG 11.32

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: At paramartha, however, the entire universe of names and forms (nama-roopa) is mithya — dependent appearance projected by Maya. Empirical time is sublated upon realisation of the timeless Self (Atman):

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: “There is neither death nor birth, neither a bound nor a struggling soul, neither a seeker after Liberation nor a liberated one – this is the ultimate truth.” - VC, v. 574

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 2.2 Trikaal language and the contrast with trikaalabadh

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita’s trikaal formulas (as in MU, v. 1) serve a non-dual purpose: Brahman is not confined to one temporal phase because Brahman is the truth of all phases and also beyond them. Temporal succession belongs to vyavahara; at liberation, the Self is discovered as never truly bound by birth, death, or succession (The Ontology of Coexistence §2.7).

passages.heading: 2-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan uses parallel trikaal vocabulary with a different ontological commitment. In the coexistential account, trikaalabadh binds coexistence across the three times while affirming perpetual unit-activity and world-realness (jagat satat; SB, p. 48). Advaita validates time operationally but finally sublates it; Madhyasth Darshan validates time as real duration of real activity and denies that realization cancels the world. The dispute is not over whether humans live in past–present–future structure, but over whether temporal becoming has final ontological weight.

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: Mainstream science answers questions about time through relativity, thermodynamics, and cosmology — not through activity-based ontology. Those models nonetheless form the main comparative partners for Madhyasth Darshan’s kaal.

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: 3.1 Spacetime and the block universe

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: In Newtonian mechanics, time was an absolute, uniform background. Einstein’s Special and General Relativity showed that time is relative to the observer’s frame and inextricably woven with space into a four-dimensional manifold: spacetime. In General Relativity, spacetime is dynamical — it can expand, curve, and in some models exhibit local beginnings (The Ontology of Coexistence §4.3).

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: A common philosophical interpretation is the block universe: past, present, and future coexist statically as coordinates in a four-dimensional block. The flow of time is treated as a feature of consciousness or description, not as an objective passage; there is no privileged “now” in the block itself.

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: 3.2 McTaggart, A-theory, B-theory, eternalism, and presentism

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: J.M.E. McTaggart’s 1908 analysis distinguishes an A-series (events as past, present, or future) from a B-series (events as earlier or later than one another). A-theories — including presentism and some growing-block models — treat the present (or the present’s passage) as ontologically special. B-theories — including eternalism and many block-universe readings — treat temporal order as relations among equally real events without a moving “now.”

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s present-centred activity ontology is A-theoretic in spirit: the present is where kriya actualises. It is not, however, a standard presentism, because past activity leaves real traces (configuration, record, and — in humans — chitta/sanskar reckoning) and future states are real anticipations rooted in present shram–gati–parinam activity rather than empty non-entities. Eternalism and the block universe are the clearest rivals: they treat temporal passage as derivative or illusory, whereas Madhyasth Darshan treats ongoing activity as the bedrock of kaal.

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: 3.3 Relational time

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: Relational theories (Leibniz, Mach, and contemporary physicists such as Carlo Rovelli) deny that time exists as an independent container. Time is the network of changes and relations among physical systems; we measure it by comparing one variable’s change to another (clock hands relative to the sun, atomic transitions relative to laboratory standards).

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s definition of kaal as duration of activity is structurally close to relational time: no freestanding temporal substance, only durations of transforming units. The difference is ontological scope — Madhyasth Darshan includes sentient unit-activity and ties duration to shram–gati–parinam across orders of nature, not only to physical observables in spacetime.

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: Whitehead’s process philosophy shares that relational realism and treats time as internal to becoming. His basic units are “actual entities” — “drops of experience, complex and interdependent” (Whitehead 1929, p. 28). Process metaphysics is a partial affinity with activity-based kaal: change and duration belong to unit-becoming, not to an absolute container. The contrast remains persistence: Whitehead’s occasions are momentary and “perpetually perish” subjectively, gaining “objective immortality” only as data for successors (Whitehead 1929, p. 44), whereas Madhyasth Darshan’s jeevan is a persisting immortal individual and insentient units retain configuration through transformation rather than subjective perishing (The Ontology of Coexistence §3.6.4).

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: 3.4 Cosmological time and beginningless existence

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: Cosmology asks whether the physical universe has a beginning. The standard ΛCDM model implies a hot big bang roughly 13.8 billion years ago; research programs in loop quantum cosmology, conformal cyclic cosmology, and eternal inflation explore whether a beginningless substrate may underlie local cosmic epochs (The Ontology of Coexistence §4.2).

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan holds that existence (astitva) is beginningless and endless, while configurations of units undergo ceaseless transformation. That claim is conceptually resonant with beginningless cosmological models and with conservation-based physics, but it is not established by them. The darshan’s further claims — immortal jeevan, order-specific cycles, activity eternally present — remain metaphysical assertions distinct from current cosmological evidence.

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: 3.5 Entropy and the arrow of time

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: Thermodynamics explains the macroscopic arrow of time — why eggs break but un-break, and why we remember the past rather than the future — through increasing entropy in closed systems (Second Law). Memory and causation align with the entropy gradient in the human branch of physical history.

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan does not derive the arrow of time from entropy; its present-centrism is compatible with thermodynamic asymmetry rather than competing with it. Within the darshan, temporal direction comes from the ontology of activity itself — but in modes that must not be conflated. Insentient units change through shram–gati–parinam (effort–motion–result): the three are inseparable joint forms of the same activity, and insentient exchange also exhibits cyclical restoration and give–take complementarity (SB, pp. 52–53, 58; The Ontology of Coexistence §1.2). Sentient jeevan uses the same triad, read toward constitutional, activity, and conduct completeness through projection, reflection, and samadhan — qualitative change without physicochemical parinam (SB, p. 55). Development (vikas) across the four orders — material, bio, animal, and knowledge — adds a further directional structure: a seed developing into a tree illustrates real order-specific transformation, not mere statistical fluctuation.

passages.heading: 3-modern-physics-and-philosophy-of-time
passages.section: 3. Modern Physics and Philosophy of Time
passages.text: The darshan therefore offers a partial ontological orientation toward temporal asymmetry — present-centred kriya, directional vikas, and (in humans) sanskar-mediated carry-forward — without replacing thermodynamics. Whether shram–gati–parinam, order-specific vikas, or sentient samadhan could formally ground or constrain entropy asymmetry remains an open question (§6.4). What Madhyasth Darshan adds in any case is an account of what time is (duration of activity) and where becoming is real (unit kriya now).

passages.heading: 4-comparative-summary
passages.text: 4. Comparative Summary

passages.heading: 4-comparative-summary
passages.text: The three frameworks agree that humans live with past–present–future structure and measurable duration. They disagree over what time is, whether the ground of reality is timeless, and whether temporal becoming is finally real.

passages.heading: 4-comparative-summary
passages.text: Question Madhyasth Darshan Advaita Vedanta Modern physics and philosophy of time What is time? Duration of unit-activity (kriya); rachna/vistar for matter-bounds; relative truth alongside direction and place Structural feature of vyavahara; mithya at paramartha Coordinate of spacetime, relational change, or thermodynamic/process parameter Is the ground timeless? Yes — satta is kriya-shunya; omnipresent at all times without kaal as activity-duration Yes — Brahman is outside temporal becoming Spacetime itself may be dynamical; “timeless” laws are model-dependent Past / present / future Present activity ontologically central; past/future traced to kriya; trikaalabadh on coexistence; atma mediative across three times Trikaal encompassed and transcended in Brahman; empirical succession valid at vyavahara Eternalism/block: all equally real; presentism/A-theory: present privileged; B-series: earlier/later only Measurement Numerical reckoning is human convention within existence (relative truth) Time valid operationally at empirical level Coordinate choice, clock standards, observer-dependent intervals World and change World perpetually real; change is real activity World mithya; change finally sublated Physical change real; passage of time disputed Closest affinity Relational/process time (Rovelli, Whitehead); present-centred activity Timeless non-dual ground with empirical temporality Relational time and some process views; tension with activity-based presentism

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5. Critical Review

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5.1 Madhyasth Darshan — activity-based time, present-centred realism

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths. The definition of kaal through kriya is internally consistent with the darshan’s coexistential ontology: timeless satta, active ikai, no freestanding temporal container. The three-truth framework situates kaal as relative truth alongside direction and place while preserving real activity-duration. Trikaalabadh on coexistence and atma’s mediative presence across the three times answer part of the Advaita challenge without sublating the world. The account of “activity eternally present” (JVD, p. 85) gives a distinctive present-centred perspective that resists both block eternalism and world-denying non-dualism. Numerical reckoning as convention aligns measurement with human epistemology while preserving real duration.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses. The relation between “every numerical moment is present as activity” and ordinary memory, anticipation, and historical record needs tighter formalisation — especially versus eternalism and versus Advaita’s turiya witness of temporal states (The Ontology of Coexistence §2.2). The darshan suggests directional structure through vikas and the activity triads but does not derive thermodynamic asymmetry from them or fully reconcile activity-based kaal with relativistic spacetime and cosmological horizons. Public evidence standards remain those of metaphysics, not laboratory physics.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan offers a coherent activity-based temporal ontology grounded in its texts, but its strongest claims about present-centred causation and beginningless coexistence remain to be tested against rival philosophies of time and against physical theory in detail.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5.2 Advaita Vedanta — timeless absolute, robust empirics

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths. Advaita integrates trikaal language with a rigorous distinction between empirical order and absolute truth. Time is not ignored: it governs vyavahara, ethics, and cosmic dissolution (BG 11.32). The Mandukya analysis of waking, dream, and deep sleep offers a first-person route into how temporal states appear and are witnessed.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses. From the Madhyasth perspective, sublating time at paramartha makes it harder to give final ontological weight to relationships, nature, and conduct — even though vyavahara is law-governed and ethically binding (The Ontology of Coexistence §6.3). Advaita’s reply that ethics deepens at realization is substantial; the dispute is over whether world-realness at every order matches Madhyasth Darshan’s standard.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Advaita is strongest where it treats temporal experience as a ladder toward timeless witness-consciousness; it is weaker as a realist ontology of perpetual unit-activity and coexistence across the three times.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5.3 Modern physics and philosophy of time — precision without agreement

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths. Relativity and thermodynamics supply precise, testable accounts of intervals, horizons, and entropy gradients. Relational and process philosophies share structural affinities with activity-based duration. McTaggart’s A/B distinction clarifies where Madhyasth Darshan sits among presentism, eternalism, and block models.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses. Physics does not settle whether the block universe, presentism, or a relational variant is true — interpretations of quantum gravity and cosmology remain contested. Relativity’s spacetime is not the same object as Madhyasth Darshan’s kaal; mapping one to the other risks category error. Entropy explains asymmetry but not the metaphysical status of “now” or of unit-activity.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Modern science is indispensable for measurement and dynamical law; it does not by itself answer what time is in the Madhyasth or Advaita sense, nor does it validate immortal jeevan or timeless Omnipresence.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems
passages.text: 6. Open Problems

passages.heading: 6-open-problems
passages.text: The mechanisms of the past in jeevan and jada. While the past survives physically in jada configurations and, in humans, is reckoned through chitta (MVD, p. 327) and carried forward through sanskar, formalising how jeevan accesses physical traces without dualism requires deeper work — to be developed alongside Philosophy-Of-Mind-And-Jeevan — particularly when comparing against block-universe models that treat the past as statically real rather than dependent.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems
passages.text: Trikaalabadh, atma, and Advaita trikaal. Both traditions use three-time language. In the coexistential account, trikaalabadh binds coexistence across the three times (SB, p. 48) and atma exists as mediative activity across the three times (MVD, p. 299). A fuller treatment must state whether these claims are logically independent of Advaita’s sublation, or whether the vocabularies only appear parallel in English.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems
passages.text: Relativity and activity-based kaal. If kaal is duration of unit-activity and numerical reckoning is conventional, how should one read coordinate time in General Relativity, horizon effects, and the block-universe interpretation? Is spacetime a useful human reckoning on large-scale activity, or a rival ontology?

passages.heading: 6-open-problems
passages.text: Entropy and the activity triad. While directional vikas across orders and the single shram–gati–parinam triad with its sentient unfolding offer partial orientation toward temporal asymmetry compatible with thermodynamics, it remains unsettled whether this structure could formally ground or mathematically constrain entropy asymmetry in physical systems, or whether mapping it directly is a category mistake.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems
passages.text: Cosmological beginning and beginningless existence. Resonance between beginningless coexistence and some cosmological models is conceptual, not evidential. What would distinguish Madhyasth Darshan’s claim from eternal inflation or cyclic cosmology on public grounds?

passages.heading: 6-open-problems
passages.text: Evidence and operational criteria. Duration of activity is objective within the darshan, but constitutional completeness and jeevan-mediated activity are not presently measurable in physics. Until operational criteria exist, the temporal ontology stands as metaphysics compatible with conservation principles, not as established science.

passages.heading: 6-open-problems
passages.text: Immortal jeevan and the experience of kaal. Because jeevan undergoes qualitative change through samadhan (resolution) rather than physicochemical parinam, it is constitutionally complete (gathanpurna) and immortal (The Ontology of Coexistence §§1.7.1, 1.8). Kaal still applies to jeevan as duration of activity — the question is not whether an immortal unit has time, but how the qualitative experience of duration for jeevan differs from insentient units undergoing shram–gati–parinam and from the decaying body (shareer) whose configurations transform through roopantaran rather than annihilation. Exploring that difference remains a future area of inquiry alongside Philosophy-Of-Mind-And-Jeevan.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Appendix: Quick Glossary

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Key terms from §§1–3 are collected here for quick reference. Each term is also defined where it first appears in the exposition.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §1

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Time (kaal) The duration of unit-activity (kriya). Not an independent cosmic dimension or container. Composition (rachna) The bounds or duration of matter as a measured object — distinct from kaal as activity-duration (MVD, p. 196). Expanse (vistar) The span of a composition — duration at the level of bounded matter, not freestanding space-time (MVD, p. 196). Relative truth One of three truth kinds in Madhyasth Darshan: direction, time, and place — with kaal as human numerical reckoning of activity-duration (SB, pp. 65, 251). Omnipresence (satta) The all-pervasive, formless, non-transforming ground. Timeless because actionless (kriya-shunya). Unit (ikai) A countable, bounded entity in nature. All units are active; hence duration applies to them. Existence (astitva) Coexistence (saha-astitva) of formless satta and active units (ikai). Beginningless and endless. Numerical reckoning Human conventional measurement of duration through mathematics. Duration is real; quantification is conventional. Trikaalabadh Binding across the three times (past, present, future). Coexistence is a timeless truth valid across all three times (SB, p. 48).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §2

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Vyavahara / Paramartha Advaita Vedanta’s distinction between the empirical order (where time is operationally valid) and absolute truth (where only timeless Brahman exists).

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Terms in §3

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning A-theory / B-theory McTaggart’s A-series (past/present/future) and B-series (earlier/later). A-theories privilege a moving or objective present; B-theories treat temporal order without an ontologically special “now.” Eternalism / presentism Eternalism: past, present, and future events are equally real (often linked to block-universe readings). Presentism: only the present exists; past and future are unreal or dependent. Block universe Interpretation of relativity on which past, present, and future coexist statically in four-dimensional spacetime.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Editorial Notes

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Three-time formulations across primary sources (§1.4, §2.2, §6.2). Samadhanatmak Bhautikvad (SB, p. 48) applies trikaalabadh (uncontradicted across the three times) to the harmony of consciousness and matter in coexistence as a whole, while Madhyasth Darshan — Co-existentialism (MVD, p. 299) locates unchanging mediative activity across the three times in atma, realised in atma and understood in buddhi. Section 1.4 presents these as complementary levels of the same coexistential account — cosmic coexistence and the sentient core through which unchanging existence is realised — rather than treating them as competing definitions.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Present-centred activity and numerical duration (§1.5, §1.6). The exposition synthesises the definition of kaal as activity-duration (MVD, pp. 34, 196; SB, p. 65), relative truth as direction, time, and place (SB, pp. 65, 251), and the public-discourse formulation that every numerical moment taken as past or future is studiable as present activity (JVD, p. 85).
